items.title: Apple’s Private Find My People Reversed to Decrypt Live Shared Locations on Linux
items.summary: A security researcher has successfully reverse-engineered Apple’s private Find My People protocol, demonstrating that a Linux machine can register with Apple’s internal services, receive an existing location-sharing key, and decrypt a friend’s live location without ever touching a Mac or iPhone. The project began innocently: the researcher wanted to build Discord geofence alerts using location data a friend was already sharing via Apple’s Find My app. What looked like a simple authenticated API call turned into roughly a week of reverse-engineering Apple’s private device-identity and messaging infrastructure, since no prior open-source project had fully replicated the flow. Using decompilations of Apple’s fmfd , findmylocated , and searchpartyd daemons alongside open-source tools like FindMy.py and pypush, the researcher rebuilt the entire pipeline field by field. Faking an Apple Device From Scratch The first hurdle was authentication. Standard iCloud login tokens returned 401 errors against the old Find My Friends API, because each Apple service issues its own scoped credentials through a broker exchange. After authenticating via GrandSlam, Apple’s account login protocol, the researcher obtained a delegate token for IDS, Apple’s private identity and encrypted-messaging layer that underpins iMessage and Find My alike. Turning that token into a working device identity required a certificate signing request with very specific, undocumented constraints: a 2048-bit RSA key, a SHA-1 signature, and a common name derived from the SHA-1 hash of the account’s profile ID, wrapped in a gzip-compressed XML property list. Registering as a Find My device was equally particular, requiring enrollment under Apple’s “alloy” multiplexer service with six specific sub-services rather than registering Find My Friends directly. The most conceptually tricky part was convincing Apple to send the encryption key for an already-accepted share to the new Linux “device.” According to a Zerotistic researcher , a SubscribeAndFetch request with an intent of distributeKeys triggers the sharing device to redistribute its current key over Apple Push Notification Service, wrapped in a signed, ECDH-verified envelope called pair-ec . Critically, this required no resharing or account changes, since Apple’s architecture is designed to hand existing keys to newly added devices automatically. The delivered key turned out to use elliptic-curve cryptography on the P-224 curve, distinct from the P-256 keys used in the messaging envelope itself. With that per-share key in hand, the researcher queried Apple’s SearchParty service, which stores encrypted location reports, and decrypted the ciphertext locally using ECDH key exchange and AES-GCM. The result: a live, verified coordinate, accuracy radius, and timestamp for the consenting friend’s device, obtained entirely through Linux tooling. The exercise didn’t uncover a security flaw that Apple would need to patch, since it only accessed a location already voluntarily shared with the researcher’s account. Its value lies instead in documenting, for the first time in detail, how Apple’s private IDS and SearchParty protocols distribute and rotate location-sharing keys, information useful to researchers building interoperable or self-hosted Find My clients. items.title: Hackers Exploit TrueConf Servers to Push Malware Through Legitimate Video Conference Downloads
items.summary: Kaspersky researchers investigating attacks on Russian organizations discovered that legitimate TrueConf video conferencing client installers were secretly bundled with PhantomCore malware , a tool associated with the Head Mare APT group. The malicious installers were distributed directly from a TrueConf server belonging to the victim organization, making the attack especially deceptive since employees believed they were downloading trusted software. The attackers chained two vulnerabilities, tracked internally as KLCERT-26-057 and KLCERT-26-058, to execute arbitrary code on TrueConf servers. Hackers Exploit TrueConf Servers The first flaw allowed an unauthenticated attacker to connect to port 4307/TCP and call an undocumented function to run a malicious script. The second vulnerability let attackers break out of an isolated execution environment and run code with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges, granting full control of the server. With system-level access, attackers replaced a legitimate server file with a malicious web shell , which they used to map the victim’s IT infrastructure, gain privileged database access, and replace legitimate client installers with infected ones. On Windows systems, they installed backdoor services named SysExcSvc and SysReadSvc that communicated via Microsoft OneDrive as a command-and-control channel. On Linux systems, attackers deployed a separate backdoor that hides its files, intercepts TrueConf network traffic, and uses GitHub for command-and-control. Anyone joining a video call hosted on a compromised server received a prompt urging them to download a new client application. That installer quietly deployed the legitimate TrueConf client alongside a hidden PhantomCore payload disguised as a DLL, granting attackers remote command execution and full control over the infected workstation. A registry key was created to ensure the malware automatically launched at every system startup. Kaspersky warns that even organizations not running TrueConf servers could be affected if employees join meetings hosted on compromised third-party or contractor servers. TrueConf fixed both vulnerabilities in server versions 5.3.9, 5.4.9, and 5.5.5, released on June 18, 2026. Kaspersky noted that internal analysis found every TrueConf server version released since 2022 was vulnerable before the patch. The vendor is actively notifying administrators to update immediately, while Kaspersky continues coordinating disclosure and remediation support. Security teams should update TrueConf servers to the patched versions immediately and scan environments for indicators of compromise that Kaspersky published , including specific file hashes, suspicious file paths, malicious domains, and unusual service names such as SysExcSvc and SysReadSvc. items.title: Google Chrome 151 Chromoting Flaw Allows Attackers to  Execute Malicious Code Remotely
items.summary: Google has released Chrome 151 Stable, fixing seven security vulnerabilities, including a critical use-after-free flaw in Chromoting that could potentially allow remote code execution. The update is rolling out as version 151.0.7922.173/.174 for Windows and macOS, and version 151.0.7922.173 for Linux. The most severe issue is tracked as CVE-2026-76017 and affects Chromoting, the technology used by Chrome Remote Desktop. Google classified the vulnerability as critical and described it as a use-after-free bug. The issue was reported internally by Google on June 11, 2026. Use-after-free vulnerabilities occur when software continues to access memory after it has been released. If an attacker can reliably control the reused memory area, they may be able to corrupt application behavior, crash the browser, disclose sensitive information, or execute attacker-controlled code. Chrome 151 Fixes Critical Chromoting Flaw In this case, the affected component is Chromoting, making the flaw especially significant in environments that use Chrome Remote Desktop. Google has not released technical details, proof-of-concept code, exploitation prerequisites, or information about active exploitation. The company said bug information may remain restricted until most Chrome users have installed the security update. This is a standard protection measure intended to reduce the likelihood of attackers weaponizing a vulnerability before organizations and individuals can patch affected systems. Chrome 151 also addresses six high-severity vulnerabilities across several browser components. These include CVE-2026-76018, a privilege-escalation flaw in Import; CVE-2026-76019, an incorrect-authorization issue in Workers; and CVE-2026-76020, a race condition in the V8 JavaScript engine. The release further fixes CVE-2026-76021, another use-after-free vulnerability in the Document Object Model component. DOM bugs can be security-relevant because web content interacts heavily with browser rendering and scripting functions. Google also patched CVE-2026-76022, a buffer overflow in the Network component, and CVE-2026-76023, an improper resource control flaw in Linux Toolkit Theming. Chrome processes untrusted web content, JavaScript, images, downloads, and remote resources every day. Vulnerabilities in browser components can therefore provide a route for attackers to compromise endpoint systems through malicious websites, advertisements, phishing links , or crafted web content. Organizations should prioritize updating Chrome on managed Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints. Administrators should verify browser version deployment via endpoint management platforms and ensure that systems restart Chrome when necessary, as users may continue running an older, vulnerable process until the browser is relaunched. Users can manually check for the update by opening Chrome, navigating to Settings, selecting About Chrome, and allowing the browser to download the latest available release. After installation, Chrome should be restarted to activate the fixes. Google credited security researchers and internal teams for identifying vulnerabilities during the development cycle. The Chromium project also relies on security testing technologies such as AddressSanitizer, MemorySanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, Control Flow Integrity, libFuzzer, and AFL to identify flaws before they reach stable releases. items.title: China-Linked Spy Campaign Uses Five New Malware Families Against Central Asian Governments
items.summary: Central Asian government bodies have been targeted in a cyberespionage operation using a compact but varied set of remote access tools. The activity, tracked as SilkParasite, relied on convincing government-themed documents and trusted Windows programs to quietly place malware on victims’ systems. The campaign appears designed for intelligence collection rather than widespread disruption. Its operators used spear-phishing emails with password-protected RAR archives, then used document macros to trigger malicious code. The lures were tailored for organizations in Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and, in one case, Georgia. Bitdefender analysts identified seven malware families in the operation, including five previously undocumented tools: DriveSilkRAT, CookiETagRAT, NomadRAT, GoginRAT, and NodeEdgeRAT. The other two families were SpiceRAT and BloodAlchemy, showing that the operation blended new development with malware linked to earlier China-nexus activity. The findings underline a growing risk for public-sector networks handling economic and diplomatic decisions. Phishing lure impersonating the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Uzbekistan (Source – Bitdefender) Rather than using one noisy implant, the actors maintained several tools, changed their supporting files between builds, and used cloud services and normal-looking traffic to make investigation harder. Bitdefender said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that the cluster has a China-nexus link at medium confidence. China-Linked Spy Campaign Uses Five New Malware Families Researchers first detected the activity at a Central Asian government body around October 2025, then uncovered an operation that had been active for most of a year. The evidence includes overlap with SpiceRAT, which Cisco Talos previously linked to SneakyChef, and infrastructure associated with China Unicom. Bitdefender did not attribute SilkParasite to one specific named group, stressing that shared tools alone cannot establish control. That restraint is important for public reporting. DriveSilkRAT formed the campaign’s backbone. It used a shared Google Drive folder for commands, downloaded plugins into memory, and returned collected data through the same service. Researchers saw roughly 65 infection identifiers, although that figure is an upper bound because one computer can create more than one identifier through hardware fingerprinting. AI-generated lure (Source – Bitdefender) The remaining malware families gave operators several ways to work inside a network. CookiETagRAT concealed commands in HTTP Cookie and ETag headers, while NomadRAT and GoginRAT fetched functions only when needed. NodeEdgeRAT used a bundled Node.js runtime, and BloodAlchemy included capabilities for clipboard logging, keystroke capture, and running processes under another user’s session. The delivery chain repeatedly abused DLL sideloading, where a legitimate signed application loads a harmful library placed beside it. This same technique has appeared in an AsyncRAT sideloading campaign and makes simple file-name detections less reliable, because the visible program can be a genuine tool. Defenders Should Hunt Behavior SilkParasite shows why a low number of infections should not be mistaken for a limited threat. The group’s modular tools kept the first-stage footprint small and allowed the operators to add features later. Similar use of trusted cloud storage appeared in the C2Looper OneDrive malware update , reinforcing the need to examine suspicious activity within commonly allowed services. Researchers found traces consistent with AI-assisted coding, including leftover test functions and placeholder encryption keys, but assessed that conclusion only at medium confidence. The stronger point is operational discipline: the malware avoided conventional command servers in some cases, rotated artifacts, and used in-memory execution to reduce visible evidence. Defenders should review signed applications running from unusual staging or temporary folders, especially when an unfamiliar DLL sits beside them. Teams should also investigate outbound Google Drive connections that do not match user activity, inspect scheduled tasks, and build baselines that expose unusual links between processes and cloud services. Recent Central Asian government backdoors show that the region remains an active espionage target. Users should treat both polished and poor-quality government-themed messages with caution. Some SilkParasite lures appeared deliberately cheap and AI-generated, meaning appearance alone is no longer a useful measure of trust. Organizations should limit macros, verify unexpected password-protected archives through a second channel, and train staff to report suspicious messages before opening attachments. items.title: Microsoft Entra ID Remote Code Execution Vulnerability Exploited in the Wild
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that a critical remote code execution flaw in Entra ID, its cloud-based identity and access management platform, has already been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-69836 , was disclosed on August 20, 2026, and carries the maximum severity rating of Critical, underscoring just how dangerous this bug is for organizations that rely on Entra ID to authenticate users across Microsoft 365, Azure, and countless third-party applications. At its core, CVE-2026-69836 stems from a deserialization of untrusted data issue, classified under CWE-502. In plain terms, Entra ID’s backend was found to process specially crafted data objects without properly validating them first. When an attacker sends malicious serialized data to a vulnerable endpoint, the service can be tricked into executing arbitrary code on the network, without needing any authentication or user interaction. That combination, remote exploitation plus no login required, is precisely what pushes this bug into critical territory and explains why threat actors moved quickly to weaponize it. Because Entra ID underpins single sign-on and access control for millions of enterprise tenants worldwide, a successful compromise doesn’t stay contained. An attacker who gains code execution on the identity layer could potentially pivot into connected cloud workloads, hijack authentication tokens , or manipulate access policies across an entire organization’s Microsoft ecosystem. Entra ID Vulnerability Actively Exploited Microsoft’s Security Response Center has explicitly marked this vulnerability as exploited, even though it was not publicly disclosed before the advisory dropped. That distinction matters to defenders: this wasn’t a bug hunted down by independent researchers and leaked ahead of a patch; it was discovered because Microsoft’s own telemetry or incident response teams caught real-world attack activity targeting Entra ID infrastructure. The company has not released a formal exploitability index score, labeling it “N/A,” but the confirmed in-the-wild exploitation alone should put every security team on alert. Unlike traditional CVEs that demand urgent patch deployment, CVE-2026-69836 falls into Microsoft’s cloud service CVE category. Since Entra ID is a fully managed cloud platform, Microsoft has already rolled out the fix on its own infrastructure. There are no update packages, KB articles, or configuration changes for customers to apply. Microsoft says this disclosure exists purely for transparency, giving security teams visibility into threats that touched their environment even though the fix was applied server-side before most organizations even knew the flaw existed. This approach is part of Microsoft’s broader “Toward Greater Transparency” initiative for cloud service vulnerabilities, which aims to keep customers informed about backend security incidents that previously might have gone unreported since no customer patching was involved. Microsoft credited security researcher Robert Fitzpatrick for reporting the issue through coordinated disclosure. While no direct remediation steps exist for customers, this incident is a reminder to review Entra ID sign-in logs , conditional access policies, and privileged role assignments for any signs of anomalous activity dating back to before the fix was deployed. Organizations should also treat this as a cue to tighten monitoring around identity infrastructure generally, since deserialization flaws in authentication services remain an attractive and high-impact target for sophisticated threat actors. items.title: Choosing the Right Detection Approach
items.summary: This article was co-authored by Gary Katz and Jason Deyalsingh In the prior article , we examined how Visibility, Detections, the Environment, and Threat Intelligence can each serve as starting points for identifying new detection opportunities, as well as how they can be used to filter and prioritize the detections worth pursuing. Having identified an opportunity, the next question is how best to detect it. This follow-on article delineates the different detection capabilities available to detection engineers, providing a framework for evaluating which technique is most appropriate for a given activity. There is no clear-cut answer. Different detection techniques require different types of data and levels of effort, while offering different tradeoffs in robustness, coverage, and complexity. Bianco’s Pyramid of Pain primarily focuses on atomic indicators and signatures, but today’s detection engineering discipline encompasses a much wider range of techniques for identifying malicious activity. The goal of this article is not to provide in-depth instruction on any one technique, but rather to provide detection engineers with an overview of the tools available in their toolbox, along with their strengths, limitations, and data requirements. By understanding the options available, detection engineers can make more informed decisions about which tool is best suited to the task at hand, rather than defaulting to the approach they know best. This article is also not specifically about the use of GenAI. While GenAI can support detection engineering at multiple points in the process, it does not fundamentally change the process itself; rather, it changes how that process can be implemented. We will start by grouping detections efforts into two categories: Malicious Activity: What have we seen the adversary previously do which might be applicable to our organization? Unexpected Activity: What should our systems or software be doing and what would be deemed unusual and potentially malicious These categories can be further divided into separate types of detections or activities, each of which require varying levels of effort and resources. Below we will introduce these types and identify their advantages and limitations. Then we will provide a mapping between the detection types and what source data is usually the impetus for creating them. Malicious Activity: Tool-Based Detections: These are detections usually based upon a malware signature, or network signature. These detections are mostly divorced from the procedure the adversary is performing and instead focus on the bespoke tool used by the adversary. While still important, they become less effective as adversaries have migrated more to living off the land and AI reduces the cost for building unique capabilities. Limitations: Less effective in identifying living-off-the-land activities since no malicious tool is required. Adversary can bypass signature-based detections by changing the code upon which the signature is based. Procedure-Instance Detections: We will add a layer between tool-based detections and procedure-based detections called procedure-instance detections. These detections focus on the procedure we observed the adversary perform. While tool-based detections identify the tool itself, the procedure-based detection identifies the action taken. This allows us to include adversaries using non-malicious tools for malicious purposes within this type of detection. Limitations: The adversary can alter their activity to perform a variation of the observed instance and thus avoid the detection while achieving a similar goal. Precondition and Postcondition Detections: In some circumstances, it can be easier to identify the preconditions or the postconditions to procedure rather than the procedure itself. For example, there may be multiple ways to update the Windows Registry Run key, HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run as a persistence mechanism but rather than identifying the actual procedure of updating the key, we can instead monitor Sysmon Registry Events (Events 12, 13, and 14), which capture registry object creation/deletion, registry value changes, and registry key/value renames. While detecting the preconditions or postconditions can allow us to detect multiple procedures achieving the same objective, we still need to examine whether other procedure could avoid these conditions. In the example above we identified by the postcondition any procedure an adversary would take to change the Windows Registry Run key for persistence, but a similar could be achieved without generating a RegistryEvent by simply replacing an existing executable referenced by a Windows Registry Run key. Limitations: It may be possible for the adversary to avoid the expected pre or post condition. The pre or post conditions may not be well defined or observable Behavior-Based Detections: These detections identify behaviors or patterns of activity associated with adversary activity. The individual behaviors may not be inherently malicious or may not be required to perform the malicious activity, but when considered in the aggregate, they can provide a valuable indication of malicious activity. These detections may look for specific actions performed in a specific order or could identify when an aggregate of micro-behaviors cross a threshold. Limitations: If the detection is not flexible, the adversary could alter a portion of the behavior, resulting in the false-negative. Changes in the timing or ordering of the activity could result in a false-negative The activity may occur across multiple systems, resulting in issues correlating telemetry across these devices. AI Categorization: We’re going to lump all AI/ML methods of characterization together here. Whether we are using a neural net or an LLM, we are still using some type of artificial intelligence to categorize the activity as malicious or non-malicious. This approach can result in a detection capability identifying a wider type of activity. For example, a signature-based approach can identify a single type of malware (or malware capability), while an ML based approach can identify a wide variety of malware variants using a classification approach. Limitations: Traditional ML approaches can require significant expertise, large amounts of training data and time to build and tune. Traditional ML approaches may provide a categorization without explainability LLM based approaches can have larger costs or response times LLM based approaches may not be deterministic, creating quality and testing issues Procedure-Based Detections: These detections identify the underlying steps that the adversary must take to achieve their objective. When deployed at the endpoint they usually require an understanding of the system API calls executed by any tools or scripts implementing the procedure. The tired-labs repository mentioned in the previous segment contains detection strategies for building these types of detections. While procedure-based detections are usually the most robust, they cannot always be achieved. Especially when there is an overlap between the procedure being used for malicious or non-malicious purposes. Consider one of the most prevalent initial access techniques, phishing. There is no procedure-based detection for phishing because the actions taken, clicking on a link or downloading a file, etc. overlap with legitimate user activity. Limitations: Usually require in-depth analysis to identify the underlying procedures performed by malicious tools Not all techniques have a limited number of procedures which can be used to generate a robust detection Logging may not exist to identify the chokepoint of the malicious procedure, even if it is well understood. The below diagram provides a more nuanced view of the top section Bianco’s pyramid. These delineations are made against the general detection types which is useful when determining which detection type to utilize for a task. CTID provides an approach for evaluating the robustness of individual detections. Unexpected Activity: In addition to detecting malicious activity, we can take a converse approach in identifying unexpected activity. This did not fit neatly into the above diagram, and thus was broken out separately. Anomaly detection starts with a baseline, which defines what expected activity looks like allowing us to alert when deviations from that baseline occur. Since anomaly detection is mostly divorced from how the adversary performed an activity, it can detect a wide variety of procedures or tools, including unknown ones. This is a core approach for identifying insider threat activity and has significant appeal as genAI lowers the cost for building new tooling or identifying new vulnerabilities. The approach does not come without limitations or downsides. Consider the word ‘mostly’, used above. In a simple example, anomaly detection could be used to identify exfiltration by looking for higher than normal outbound traffic. This would identify exfil irrespective of the C2 protocol, but would miss adversaries with the tradecraft to move low volume and slow, or miss those using email or other approaches for their exfil. In addition, simply because something is an anomaly, does not necessarily mean it is malicious. This can result in higher false positive rates and higher investigation times since there is little explanation for why the anomaly occurred. Limitations: Requires baselining normal activity to identify anomalous activity Higher false positive rate Limited explainability Policy Violations Each company has their own definition of how it should operate technology. Policies are governance artifacts that attempt to guide how users interact with the technical environment. Typically a policy that prohibits certain activity indicates some constraint that makes it infeasible or impossible to implement a preventative control for that activity. Threat actors, unlike internal employees, are not familiarized with internal company policies, and frequently cross these invisible governance boundaries. Designing detections around policy breaches can not only surface employees who might be using systems incorrectly, but also help identify malicious activity. Consider a fairly trivial example where you want to prevent users from cloning internal repositories from unmanaged devices. This can be difficult to control from a technical standpoint (blocking the clone operation might be unfeasible). A policy can be designed to formally prohibit the activity, but recording clone operations, as well as the source systems can be used to develop detections to alert relevant teams of policy breaches, some of which may be related to threat actor activity. Limitations: May require additional research to distinguish between internal user and malicious actor violating policy Configuration Changes When designing detections, you will encounter preventative controls that seem to eliminate the need for detective controls: — Users cannot upload files to file sharing sites because those are blocked at the proxy. — standard user workstations cannot RDP to domain controllers because it is blocked at the firewall — the local anti-virus will block any malware from being executed. It is not uncommon for threat actors, with the right valid credentials, to manipulate preventative controls which might obstruct their operation. Blocklists are modified, firewall configurations are changed, and security tools are impaired or disabled entirely. With this in mind, it is reasonable to develop detection strategies around changes to critical configurations, specifically the changes that might relax the preventative controls within the environment. Limitations: Requires deconfliction with legitimate configuration changes It is easy to get tunnel vision when creating detections day in and day out. Taking a step back and evaluating what you want to detection, as defined in our previous article, is a good first step. Identifying which detection approach to use can be equally important. Just like adversaries can be prone to reusing tools and capabilities to attack, defenders can equally find themselves returning to the same detection approach as a solution. Each approach though has their strengths and their limitations. The above breakdown provides a reference for choosing the right approach for the task, rather than falling back on familiar habits. items.title: Where do Detection Ideas Come From?
items.summary: This article was co-authored by Gary Katz and Jason Deyalsingh Recent studies have shown that genAI is commoditizing the creation of detection rules. This elevates the minimal qualifications of the detection engineer from simply creating detections to identifying where to focus efforts, implementing more robust detection capabilities and performing the research and tooling to support them. This article will focus on the first of these skillsets, identifying opportunities to create detections which align to your organization’s needs. In the previous article, Critical Asset Analysis for Detection Engineering , we looked at one approach for prioritizing tasking for a detection engineering team. In this article, we will expand upon that analysis to examine four information sources of detection engineering and how they each can be either a starting point or a filter mechanism for prioritization. In the follow on article, we will identify different detection approaches, their limitations, and their data sources. This provides a guide for starting either from the data source perspective or from the detection mechanism perspective to prioritize tasking which aligns to your organization, skillset or detection capabilities. Teams should take a balanced approach across each of these options, using the right tool in the toolbox to achieve their goal. In general, there are four information sources or categories of inputs to consider when building out a detection. Visibility: These are the logs or events which we build the detection from. We can consider the logs currently ingested into your SIEM, EDR, etc. The logs which are not ingested but could, and logs which we could have our custom software create. (When considering the third group, keep in mind the time or effort required to have your software team respond to your request) Detections: What existing detections does the team have or what third party detections can the team repurpose for their need? Environment: What is the infrastructure, network, systems, operating systems, individuals, etc. which you are protecting? Threat Intelligence / Research: Within this article, we cover the differences and value of strategic, operational and tactical threat intelligence. Our most relevant threat intelligence is as anything which tells us about how the adversary has previously implemented a procedure or how an adversary could implement a procedure. The information might come from a 3rd party threat intelligence source, internal forensic analysis of previous attacks, or research into how an attack has previously been, or could be, performed. These four sets of data can be used to determine the importance of building a detection, the effort required to build it and the potential robustness of the resulting detection. Your analysis will most likely start with one of these four categories and pivot to the others. Let’s consider each starting point and the value and limitations associated with the approach. In each case we start with gathering that type of information and then filtering down what is important based on the other three categories of data. This allows the analyst to then pivot or research to identify the additional knowledge required to create the detection. Starting with Visibility: As mentioned above, visibility is your access to events or logs which are the basis for building detections. In some circumstances, these events were created explicitly for detecting malicious activity and thus can be an easy starting point for building detections. One resource is Microsoft’s documentation which commonly provides guidance on events-to-monitor for specific infrastructure.
